methodology: The conventional reading is stated first and in full, from the field's own sources. Every factual sentence carries a note. Quotations were checked against the sources themselves where reachable: Hachtmann, International Review of Social History 55:3 (2010); Herbert, International Labor and Working-Class History 58 (2000); the USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia articles cited; the IG Farben judgment (Trials of War Criminals vol. VIII); Hayes and Allen in the USHMM 2004 symposium volume; Pohl's report to Himmler of 30 April 1942; Arendt's Origins of Totalitarianism; Nelson, Frontiers of Empire (2024); Kramer, Sandler and Adhikari as published. A reading of the draft was applied before deposit.
falsification_conditions: The argument weakens if Hachtmann's evidence for camp prisoners in regular industrial mass production (Heinkel Oranienburg from August 1942, aircraft production in early 1944) does not hold; if the racial wage, ration and segregation tiers did not follow classification as Herbert and Spoerer describe; if the replacement of selected prisoners at Monowitz and Fürstengrube is shown not to have operated as described; or if a source shows the colonial conception of the East to be absent from Nazi planning. It is not affected by the absence of a direct genealogy from colonial camps to Nazi camps or by the absence of an economic cause of the Holocaust, neither of which it claims. Any quotation found not to match its source falsifies that sentence and is to be corrected by erratum.

wiki_article:
The Colony Enters the Factory: War Fordism, Racial Labor Hierarchy, and the Industrialization of Conquest (EA-NOUN-VERB-02 v1.0), deposit #1669 of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive (7 October 2026), is the second half of a historical argument by Lee Sharks whose first half is The Noun Becomes a Verb (#1668). It opens by accepting the conventional reading: the Nazi camps were founded in 1933 as instruments of political terror; forced labor in the Reich was a vast system graded by nationality and race; historians widely accept the colonial self-understanding of the war in the East, contest a direct continuity from the Herero and Nama genocide in German South-West Africa, and reject a colonial or economic cause of the Holocaust.

Germany was an advanced industrial power constrained by scale, for which labor became a binding wartime constraint; Ulrich Herbert judges that production would have collapsed in 1942 at the latest without foreign workers. Lebensraum was conceived as continental colonization, through an institution of German inner colonization older than Nazism that Robert Nelson traces to the Prussian Settlement Commission, and the empire pursued for land and racial reordering also became a mechanism for supplying labor: territory moved outward and labor moved inward. Rüdiger Hachtmann's war Fordism decomposed work into simplified operations while the racial state decomposed persons into graded classes of wage, ration and segregation; his aptitude tests show the instruments of measurement crossing the racial grade.

From the second half of 1942 the camp was attached to the factory, a form the paper calls campification, held at Hachtmann's scale: a minority of camp prisoners in industrial production from late 1942 to mid-1944, with construction for underground relocation in the war's final months. At the factory camps the prisoner's working day was allocated by the state for a daily fee and replenished by conquest and deportation, a third relation beside the owned person and the contracted interval of the first half. Racial-juridical classification acted as a switch that set the permissible range of coercion under which the industrial operation was extracted.

The paper does not reduce the Holocaust to labor economics. With Peter Hayes and Christopher Browning it holds that extermination and exploitation sometimes reinforced and sometimes destroyed each other's objects, that labor deferred the murder for some only for a time, and that the murder of the Jews of Europe is larger than the labor history it tells. It treats the colonial camps of 1900 as a shared repertoire, following Alan Kramer's caution against a straight genealogy, and closes on Arendt's continental imperialism: the colony entered the factory.

defines_concepts.definition: The attachment of the concentration camp to the industrial plant as an administrative unit: a subcamp in or near the factory, supplied with prisoners by a main camp, run by the SS and contracted to a firm, with its form set in the second half of 1942 and its network spread in 1944. Held at the scale Hachtmann gives: a minority of camp prisoners in industrial production, late 1942 to mid-1944.

The Nazi recombination of the first half's grammar: the industrial operation (the verb) stays divisible, measurable and standardized, while racial-juridical classification (the noun) sets the permissible range of compulsion, deprivation and violence under which it is extracted; the same reading of productive capacity carries radically different consequences by status.

The third relation to the person beside the owned noun of chattel slavery and the contracted verb of wage labor: the state holds the prisoner by confinement, a firm pays a daily fee for the prisoner's working day, and the workforce is treated as a flow drawn from a captured population, reduced by death and refilled by deportation. The holder does not bear the chattel owner's capital loss in the person as owned property.

Arendt's continental imperialism read as a labor geography: with no distance between the methods of colony and nation, territory moved outward while conquered populations were carried inward to the industrial core, so that the colony entered the factory.
